text: This phone is five point two millimeters thick. Thinner than any iPhone before it. And it folds in half.

To make glass bend without breaking, and carry power and heat across a moving joint, it takes a hinge with over a hundred parts, a ten-layer screen, and two separate batteries. So let's take it apart. Every part, every layer, all the way down to the atoms.
This is the iPhone Duo. Closed, it's a phone you can hold in one hand. Open it, and it becomes a seven point six inch screen. The largest display ever put in an iPhone.
That inner screen is wide and short, about one point four to one. So a widescreen video fills much more of it than it would on a square folding screen.
To fold, the phone is split into two halves, each just over five millimeters thick, wrapped in a titanium frame. Everything a normal phone carries has to fit inside that space.
Each half has its own battery. The rear cameras sit on one side. A five point four inch outer screen sits on the back of the other. And holding them together is the hinge.

Compared with a regular iPhone, a few things move around. There's no Face ID: you unlock it with Touch ID in the side button. The volume buttons sit on the top edge. The outer screen is shaped like a D, square by the hinge and rounded on the outside, with its controls down the right edge. And the USB-C port sits low on the left half, out of the way when you use it like a laptop. Inside, it runs the same A20 Pro chip as the iPhone 18 Pro.

Every time you open it, dozens of parts move together in less than a second. So we'll follow that one moment through the phone: the hinge turning, the screen bending, power and heat crossing from one half to the other, and the phone waking up. It starts with the hinge.
